items.english: Another was a monk in a yellow robe, with a small bronze ring hung from his ear, of a strangely antique visage at first sight. His skin was dark beyond the common, and, to see the curl of his hair and beard, he seemed a man come from somewhere west of the Congling. For some time he had been patiently flourishing a red-handled fly-whisk to drive off the horseflies and flies that would fasten upon the naked man, but, grown a little tired at last, as it seemed, he had now come beside that same unglazed jar and squatted there ceremoniously, in the attitude of a turkey.
notes: Congling kept as transliterated proper noun; understood as the Onion Range west of China, marking the monk as from the Western Regions. Left for note rather than glossed in text.
Fly-whisk renders shubi: a priestly implement of horsehair with ornamented handle, here red-handled, used to shoo insects. Kept flat, not ennobled.
Like a turkey kept as the low, faintly unflattering comparison it is; not softened.

items.english: The last stood far apart from the other two, under the eaves of a thatched hut in the corner of the threshing-yard. This man grew on the tip of his chin, by way of apology, a beard like a rat's tail, and his get-up was a hemp robe long enough to hide his heels, with a tea-brown sash whose knot hung slack. From the careful way he plied from time to time a fan made of white birds' feathers, he was probably a Confucian scholar or something of the sort.
notes: Sobusan and sakattai rendered descriptively as hemp robe and tea-brown sash; the Japanese terms specify plain literati dress, not transliterated here to keep the tableau readable.
White-feather fan kept literal; it is the mark by which this figure will later be known as Sun Sensei, but here the narrator only conjectures scholar.

items.english: All three alike kept their mouths shut as if by agreement. Nor did they so much as stir, as though they took some uncommon interest in whatever was about to happen, and for that held their breath.

data.say: Drafted p4-p6 as held tableau, keeping the foreign monk, the scholar, and the shut-mouthed stillness flat and unmoved.
